### Impact The BER decoder (shared by the CER and DER codecs) parses long-form tags by accumulating continuation octets in a loop with no upper bound on the size of the tag ID. A crafted input can force the decoder to build an arbitrarily large integer, with CPU cost growing quadratically in input size — a ~1 MB input consumes over a minute of CPU. On Python 3.11+, the oversized tag ID can also trigger an unhandled `ValueError` (integer string conversion limit) while the decoder formats error messages, violating the documented `PyAsn1Error` contract and potentially bypassing caller error handling.  Any application decoding untrusted BER/CER/DER input is affected.  ### Affected components - `pyasn1.codec.ber.decoder` — `decode()` and `StreamingDecoder` - `pyasn1.codec.cer.decoder` and `pyasn1.codec.der.decoder`, which inherit   the same tag parsing - `pyasn1.type.tag` — `Tag`/`TagSet` reprs could raise `ValueError` when   rendering oversized tag IDs (reachable through decoder error paths)  The encoders and the `pyasn1.codec.native` codec are not affected.  ### Patches Fixed in 0.6.4. Long-form tag IDs are now limited to 20 octets (140-bit tag IDs, matching the existing OID arc limit); oversized tags are rejected with `PyAsn1Error`. Tag ID rendering in reprs and error messages was additionally hardened against the interpreter's integer-to-string conversion limit.  ### Workarounds Bound the size of untrusted input passed to `decode()` before calling it.

## Summary  In pyasn1 through 0.6.4, decoding a constructed BIT STRING with many fragments repeatedly shifts and copies the entire value accumulated so far. For fixed-size fragments, CPU time grows quadratically with the encoded input size. An application that passes sufficiently large, attacker-controlled ASN.1 data to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion during `decode()`; no conversion or formatting of the decoded value is required.  The BER and CER decoders reach this path for constructed BIT STRING values, with or without an `asn1Spec`. The DER decoder rejects constructed BIT STRING in schema-less decoding, but its schema-driven path accepts a **definite-length** constructed BIT STRING when given a matching `asn1Spec` and reaches the same vulnerable code. Constructed BIT STRING is not valid DER; this DER exposure is due to decoder permissiveness. DER rejects the indefinite-length form.  This is a separate decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER accumulation fixed in [CVE-2026-59885](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj).  ## Technical details  In the 0.6.4 [`BitStringPayloadDecoder`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L173-L301), both the [definite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L237-L255) and [indefinite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L275-L301) fragment loops call `BitString.fromOctetString(..., prepend=bitString)` for every fragment. [`fromOctetString`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/type/univ.py#L614-L627) shifts the growing `SizedInteger` left by the fragment's bit length and ORs in the fragment. Shifting an ever-larger Python integer for each fixed-size fragment makes total work O(n²) for n fragments. The fragments are siblings, so the decoder's nesting-depth limit does not constrain their count; its limit on the number of length octets does not prevent the demonstrated inputs.  In 0.6.4, DER's [tag-driven map](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L15-L40) disables constructed BIT STRING, while its schema-driven type map retains the inherited decoder that permits it. This explains why a schema-less DER rejection is not a negative result for all DER decoding.  Under [X.690](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en), a conforming CER constructed BIT STRING uses an indefinite-length outer encoding and primitive fragments with 1000 contents octets except possibly the last. That form reaches the affected indefinite-length loop. DER requires primitive string encoding, although the schema-driven pyasn1 decoder accepts the definite-length constructed example below.  ## Impact  An application is exposed when untrusted input can reach one of the affected decoder paths and its input limits admit enough fragments. The work occupies the decoding thread or worker and may cause denial of service. Whether the input is network-accessible or unauthenticated depends on the calling application. This advisory makes no claim that every application using pyasn1, or any particular protocol implementation, accepts such input.  ## Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)  The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER values trigger the issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted values could occupy a finite decoder-worker pool and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not claim that every application is network-exposed or fully unavailable; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See [FIRST's library-scoring guidance](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/user-guide).  ## Reproducer  The definite-length example below is valid BER. It is deliberately not a conforming CER or DER encoding. The second constructor uses conforming CER fragment sizing and framing. CPU times are machine-dependent; run the larger cases only in a local test environment.  ```python import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber_decoder from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer_decoder from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der_decoder from pyasn1.error import PyAsn1Error from pyasn1.type import univ   def encode_length(size):     octets = size.to_bytes((size.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")     return bytes((0x80 | len(octets),)) + octets   def definite_fragments(count):     body = b"\x03\x02\x00\xa5" * count  # one data octet per BIT STRING fragment     return b"\x23" + encode_length(len(body)) + body   def cer_fragments(count):     # Each primitive fragment has 1000 contents octets: one unused-bits     # octet (zero) followed by 999 data octets.     fragment = b"\x03" + encode_length(1000) + b"\x00" + b"\xa5" * 999     return b"\x23\x80" + fragment * count + b"\x00\x00"   def measure(label, decode, payload, **options):     start = time.process_time()     value, remainder = decode(payload, **options)     print(label, len(payload), f"{time.process_time() - start:.3f}s CPU")     assert not remainder and len(value) > 0   for count in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):     measure(f"BER {count} fragments", ber_decoder.decode,             definite_fragments(count))  for count in (1_000, 2_000, 4_000):     measure(f"CER {count} fragments", cer_decoder.decode,             cer_fragments(count))  sample = definite_fragments(1_000) measure("DER with BIT STRING schema", der_decoder.decode, sample,         asn1Spec=univ.BitString()) try:     der_decoder.decode(sample) except PyAsn1Error:     print("DER without schema rejects the constructed value") else:     raise AssertionError("DER unexpectedly accepted schema-less input") ```  ## Verification  Local measurements of the official v0.6.4 tag on CPython 3.14.8 used `time.process_time()`. A local 0.6.5 candidate containing the fix was timed on the same machine. Times are illustrative, not a guaranteed cost on other systems.  | Input | Size | v0.6.4 CPU | 0.6.5 candidate CPU | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | BER definite, 50,000 fragments | 0.20 MB | 0.530 s | 0.084 s | | BER definite, 100,000 fragments | 0.40 MB | 1.915 s | 0.170 s | | BER definite, 200,000 fragments | 0.80 MB | 7.392 s | 0.344 s | | Conforming CER, 1,000 fragments | 1.004 MB | 0.163 s | 0.0035 s | | Conforming CER, 2,000 fragments | 2.008 MB | 0.657 s | 0.0070 s | | Conforming CER, 4,000 fragments | 4.016 MB | 2.582 s | 0.0144 s |  The definite BER input with 100,000 fragments also decoded through DER with `asn1Spec=univ.BitString()` in 1.949 s on v0.6.4, versus 0.172 s with the 0.6.5 candidate. Schema-less DER rejected the same input. Independent reports reproduced the old behavior on v0.6.4: one measured 21.1 s for a 1.28 MB definite-length value; another measured 7.25 s for a 0.8 MB value versus 2.8 ms for a primitive BIT STRING carrying the same data volume. These measurements were taken on different systems and should not be compared as a single benchmark series.  ## Resolution  Upgrade to pyasn1 0.6.5. The decoder assembles fragment bits in a `bytearray`, preserves decoded bit values including intermediate-fragment padding, and converts the complete payload to a BIT STRING once. This removes the repeated shift of the growing integer in both constructed decoding loops.  For applications that cannot upgrade immediately, enforce an application-appropriate limit on untrusted ASN.1 input size **before** passing it to pyasn1. Such a limit bounds exposure but does not change the quadratic behavior of 0.6.4. Where a protocol forbids constructed BIT STRING, rejecting that encoding before decoding also prevents this path.

### Summary  When an application decodes attacker-controlled BER, CER, or DER data without an ASN.1 schema, a container with many distinct long tag IDs can cause quadratic CPU use. Repeated inputs can exhaust CPU and reduce service availability.  ### Details  ConstructedPayloadDecoderBase._decodeComponentsSchemaless inserts every decoded component’s TagSet into a growing set, although it only needs to distinguish one tag set from two or more. Attacker-chosen tag IDs can have colliding TagSet hashes, making each later insertion compare against an increasing number of earlier tags. This path is present in v0.6.4 and is inherited by the CER and DER decoders. The proposed fix stops growing the classification set after it contains two distinct tag sets, while retaining every decoded component and its order.  On v0.6.4 with CPython 3.12.10, increasing the collision input from 3,200 to 6,400 components raised decode CPU time from 0.438 to 1.747 seconds; a comparable control rose from 0.031 to 0.065 seconds. Both inputs decoded successfully with the expected values and an empty remainder.  ### Proof of concept  Run this outside the repository checkout in a fresh Python 3.12 environment with pyasn1==0.6.4 installed:  ```python import sys import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder from pyasn1.type import univ   def enc_tag(tag_id):     groups = [tag_id & 0x7f]     tag_id >>= 7     while tag_id:         groups.append((tag_id & 0x7f) | 0x80)         tag_id >>= 7     return b'\xbf' + bytes(reversed(groups))   def payload(tag_ids):     body = b''.join(enc_tag(tag_id) + b'\x03\x04\x01A'                     for tag_id in tag_ids)     length = len(body).to_bytes((len(body).bit_length() + 7) // 8, 'big')     return b'\x30' + bytes([0x80 | len(length)]) + length + body   for count in (3200, 6400):     cases = (         ("collision", [32 + i * sys.hash_info.modulus                        for i in range(count)]),         ("control", [(1 << 70) + i for i in range(count)]),     )     for name, tag_ids in cases:         wire = payload(tag_ids)         start = time.process_time()         value, remainder = decoder.decode(wire)         cpu_seconds = time.process_time() - start          assert type(value) is univ.Sequence         assert len(value) == count and remainder == b''         for position, tag_id in enumerate(tag_ids):             component = value.getComponentByPosition(position)             assert component.asOctets() == b'A'             assert component.tagSet[-1].tagId == tag_id          print(count, name, len(wire), round(cpu_seconds, 3)) ```  ### Impact  Applications that pass attacker-controlled bytes to schemaless BER, CER, or DER decoding can spend disproportionate CPU time on a relatively small, valid input. The demonstrated impact is availability; no confidentiality or integrity impact was observed.

## Summary  In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a binary-encoded ASN.1 REAL with a large mantissa can consume CPU time quadratic in the mantissa length. The BER, CER, and DER decoders all use the affected `RealPayloadDecoder`. An application is exposed when it passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 containing a REAL value to one of these decoders, either without an `asn1Spec` or with a schema that includes REAL. The work occurs inside `decode()`; the application does not need to convert, print, or otherwise use the resulting REAL object.  This is distinct from [CVE-2026-59886](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hm4w-wwcw-mr6r), which concerns converting an already-decoded REAL to a Python float. That issue was fixed in 0.6.4 and its advisory states that decoding alone does not trigger it.  ## Root cause and affected components  For binary REAL values, [`RealPayloadDecoder.valueDecoder` in v0.6.4](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L535-L603) builds the mantissa one octet at a time:  ```python p = 0 while chunk:     p <<= 8     p |= chunk[0]     chunk = chunk[1:] ```  Each shift processes an integer that grows with the mantissa; with byte strings, each slice also copies the remaining suffix. Repeating both operations for every octet makes decoding quadratic in mantissa size. The decoder's [eight-octet length-field limit](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1704-L1717) does not impose a practical mantissa-size limit for the inputs demonstrated below. [CER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/cer/decoder.py#L51-L62) and [DER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L23-L31) reuse the BER REAL payload decoder, so all three paths reach this loop.  The vulnerable loop is present in every available repository release tag inspected, from v0.2.1 through v0.6.4. Runtime measurements below were made on v0.6.4; older releases were checked for the loop, not benchmarked individually.  ## Impact  A comparatively small REAL value can hold a decoder worker on one CPU core for seconds or longer. The attacker must be able to supply data that the application sends to an affected decoder, and application-level input limits may reduce exposure. The demonstrated effect is CPU exhaustion during decoding; this advisory does not assert a network endpoint, unauthenticated access, or an affected downstream application by itself.  ## Reproduction and evidence  The following example uses pyasn1 0.6.4. The `0x09` tag identifies REAL; `0x80 0x00` selects a positive, base-2 binary value with a one-octet zero exponent, followed by a large mantissa. It exercises `decode()` only.  ```python import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der   def real_value(mantissa_octets):     content = b"\x80\x00" + b"\xff" * mantissa_octets     length = len(content).to_bytes(3, "big")     return b"\x09\x83" + length + content   for codec in (ber, cer, der):     for size in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):         substrate = real_value(size)         started = time.process_time()         value, rest = codec.decode(substrate)         print(codec.__name__, size, time.process_time() - started)         assert not rest         assert tuple(value)[1:] == (2, 0) ```  The original report measured the following BER CPU times on repository commit `aa05757`. That commit is later than the official v0.6.4 tag; the vulnerable loop is identical in the tagged release.  | Mantissa size | Reporter's BER CPU time | | ---: | ---: | | 50,000 octets | 0.328 s | | 100,000 octets | 1.299 s | | 200,000 octets | 6.043 s | | 400,000 octets | 24.095 s |  The same report measured 5.645 s for a 200,000-octet mantissa through DER.  A separate local reproduction on the official v0.6.4 tag (`d43496f`, CPython 3.14.8, macOS arm64) measured BER at 0.209 s, 0.884 s, and 3.451 s for 50,000, 100,000, and 200,000 mantissa octets respectively. CER and DER each took about 0.89 s at 100,000 octets. These are machine-specific measurements; the repeated near-fourfold cost for doubled input is the relevant result. Neither reproduction calls `float()`, `str()`, or `prettyPrint()`.  ## Fix  pyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the per-octet shift and slice loop with one `int.from_bytes(bytes(chunk), "big")` conversion. Sign, scale, exponent, and the decoded REAL tuple are preserved. The fix is in the shared BER payload decoder and therefore covers BER, CER, and DER. A local check of the 0.6.5 candidate decoded a 200,000-octet mantissa correctly through all three codecs; the check does not establish behavior for every application using REAL.  ## Workarounds  Upgrade to pyasn1 0.6.5. Until then, reject or strictly limit attacker-controlled ASN.1 input that may contain REAL values before passing it to pyasn1. The appropriate size limit depends on the application's available CPU time and request volume.

## Summary  In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a constructed OCTET STRING or character string made of many fragments can spend disproportionate CPU time repeatedly copying the accumulated value. A separate indefinite-length `ANY` path has the same problem while collecting the encoded components. The work grows roughly quadratically with the number of fixed-size fragments, although the input and decoded value grow linearly. An application that lets an attacker supply such ASN.1 input to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion.  The affected string paths are available in BER and CER. The DER decoder also accepts certain *non-DER* constructed strings: a definite-length constructed OCTET STRING when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.OctetString`, and constructed character strings such as UTF8String even without a schema. Indefinite-length `ANY` is affected in BER and CER when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.Any`; DER rejects indefinite lengths.  This is a distinct decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER/RELATIVE-OID accumulation addressed by [CVE-2026-59885](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj). It has the same complexity class, but the OID fix in 0.6.4 did not change these string or `ANY` loops.  ## Technical details  In the [v0.6.4 BER decoder](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py), `OctetStringPayloadDecoder` appends each decoded fragment to a growing `bytes` value with `header += component` in both its [definite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L338-L351) and [indefinite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L368-L387) constructed forms. [`AnyPayloadDecoder.indefLenValueDecoder`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1403-L1430) similarly uses `chunk += component`. In the exercised paths, each concatenation copies an increasingly large prefix. For `N` fixed-size fragments, the total copied data grows with `1 + 2 + ... + N`, or O(N²).  The OCTET STRING decoder is also the base class of the decoders for UTF8String, NumericString, PrintableString, TeletexString, VideotexString, IA5String, GraphicString, VisibleString, GeneralString, UniversalString, BMPString, ObjectDescriptor, GeneralizedTime, and UTCTime. These types inherit the same constructed-string reassembly path.  The [DER decoder's OCTET STRING restriction](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L15-L49) replaces the tag-driven decoder, but its schema-driven `TYPE_MAP` retains the BER-derived decoder. Thus `der.decode(data)` rejects a constructed OCTET STRING, while `der.decode(data, asn1Spec=univ.OctetString())` accepts its definite-length form and reaches the accumulation loop. DER does not replace the inherited character-string decoders, so a constructed UTF8String is also accepted without `asn1Spec`. These inputs violate [X.690's DER string-encoding rule](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en) and should not be described as valid DER encodings.  The original short-fragment, definite-length OCTET STRING reproducer is valid BER. The CER decoder accepts it, but it is not a conforming CER string encoding: X.690 requires an indefinite-length outer constructed string and 1,000 contents octets per fragment except possibly the last. A conforming CER-shaped constructed OCTET STRING with those fragment sizes also reaches the loop and shows quadratic growth. The indefinite-length `ANY` reproducer below can represent a CER `SEQUENCE OF OCTET STRING` and reaches the separate `ANY` loop when decoded with an `ANY` schema.  The decoder's eight-octet length-field limit and nesting-depth limit do not bound the number of sibling fragments in these examples. The BER reproducer below uses only a three-octet outer length field; all fragments have shallow nesting. There is no per-message fragment-count cap in v0.6.4.  ## Impact  If an application passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 to the affected `decode()` or `StreamingDecoder` path without an adequate input or resource limit, a megabyte-scale value can occupy a decoding worker for seconds. Repeated inputs can exhaust available CPU. Whether this is reachable before authentication, or through a particular protocol, depends on the application; the library finding alone does not establish those conditions. No confidentiality or integrity impact is claimed.  ## Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)  The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER inputs trigger the string-reassembly issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted inputs could occupy all available decoder workers and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not assert that every adopter has such an endpoint or loses all service; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See [FIRST's library-scoring guidance](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/user-guide).  On the official v0.6.4 tag, local CPU-time measurements with CPython 3.14.8 on macOS arm64 gave the following results. Times vary by machine and Python runtime; the input-size scaling is the relevant observation. “Fixed” means the local 0.6.5 decoder fix applied to the same inputs.  | Decoder path and input | Fragments | v0.6.4 CPU | Fixed CPU | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | BER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.40 MB | 100,000 × 2 payload bytes | 0.340 s | 0.160 s | | BER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.80 MB | 200,000 × 2 payload bytes | 0.886 s | 0.312 s | | BER constructed OCTET STRING, 1.60 MB | 400,000 × 2 payload bytes | 2.738 s | 0.623 s | | BER indefinite `ANY`, 0.30 MB | 100,000 × 1 payload byte | 0.459 s | 0.206 s | | BER indefinite `ANY`, 0.60 MB | 200,000 × 1 payload byte | 1.245 s | 0.412 s | | BER indefinite `ANY`, 1.20 MB | 400,000 × 1 payload byte | 3.980 s | 0.826 s | | CER constructed OCTET STRING, 1.00 MB, conforming fragment layout | 1,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.0089 s | 0.0022 s | | CER constructed OCTET STRING, 2.01 MB, conforming fragment layout | 2,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.0311 s | 0.0044 s | | CER constructed OCTET STRING, 4.02 MB, conforming fragment layout | 4,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.1379 s | 0.0090 s |  For the same short-fragment layout, the original report measured up to 16.05 seconds for a 3.2 MB BER constructed OCTET STRING. An independent report on CPython 3.11.16/Linux measured 5.76 seconds for a 2.4 MB constructed OCTET STRING, versus about 0.005 seconds for a primitive OCTET STRING of comparable size. These are reporter measurements on different systems, not fixed performance guarantees.  ## Reproduction  This example uses public decoder APIs. Run it with pyasn1 0.6.4 and increase `n` to observe the scaling. The final two calls show the DER paths accepted by v0.6.4; their constructed encodings are not valid DER.  ```python import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der from pyasn1.type import univ   def tlv(identifier, contents):     length = len(contents)     if length < 128:         return bytes((identifier, length)) + contents     encoded = length.to_bytes((length.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")     return bytes((identifier, 0x80 | len(encoded))) + encoded + contents   def measure(label, decode, substrate, asn1Spec=None):     start = time.process_time()     _, rest = decode(substrate, asn1Spec=asn1Spec)     assert not rest     print(f"{label}: {len(substrate)} input bytes, "           f"{time.process_time() - start:.3f} CPU seconds")   n = 100_000 octet_fragments = b"\x04\x02AA" * n utf8_fragments = b"\x0c\x02AA" * n  measure("BER constructed OCTET STRING", ber.decode,         tlv(0x24, octet_fragments)) measure("BER indefinite ANY", ber.decode,         b"\x30\x80" + b"\x04\x01A" * n + b"\x00\x00",         univ.Any())  # CER uses indefinite length and 1,000-content-octet primitive fragments. cer_fragment = tlv(0x04, b"A" * 1000) measure("CER constructed OCTET STRING", cer.decode,         b"\x24\x80" + cer_fragment * 1000 + b"\x00\x00")  # These constructed encodings are accepted by pyasn1 but are invalid DER. measure("DER OCTET STRING with schema", der.decode,         tlv(0x24, octet_fragments), univ.OctetString()) measure("DER UTF8String without schema", der.decode,         tlv(0x2c, utf8_fragments)) ```  ## Patch  pyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the growing `bytes` accumulator with a list of fragments and joins them once after decoding in all three affected loops. The OCTET STRING base-class change also covers the inheriting character-string decoders. This removes the repeated copying while preserving the assembled decoded value.  ## Workaround  Until upgrading, enforce application-appropriate limits on the size of untrusted ASN.1 input *before* passing it to pyasn1, and limit the CPU resources available to decoding workers. Applications that require DER can also reject constructed string encodings before invoking the decoder. The appropriate byte limit depends on the protocol and expected valid values.  ## Credits and references  Reported by [alimony](https://github.com/alimony). Independently reported by [manus-pi](https://github.com/manus-pi), whose report identified the schema-driven DER route, inherited character-string decoders, and additional performance evidence.  - [pyasn1 v0.6.4 affected decoder source](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py) - [ITU-T X.690, CER and DER string-encoding rules](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en) - [CVE-2026-59885, separate OID decoder issue](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj)

setuptools is a package that allows users to download, build, install, upgrade, and uninstall Python packages. Prior to 83.0.0, FileList applied MANIFEST.in exclude, global-exclude, recursive-exclude, and prune directives by matching compiled glob patterns against on-disk file names without Unicode normalization, so on macOS APFS or HFS+ an NFD file name could bypass an NFC exclusion rule and be packed into a source distribution. This issue is fixed in version 83.0.0.

## Summary  When building a source distribution (`python -m build --sdist` / `setup.py sdist`), setuptools' `FileList` applies `MANIFEST.in` directives (`exclude`, `global-exclude`, `recursive-exclude`, `prune`) by matching a compiled glob against on-disk file names **byte-for-byte, with no Unicode normalization**. On normalization-preserving filesystems (notably macOS APFS and HFS+), a file written in NFD and a `MANIFEST.in` rule written in NFC refer to the same file but are byte-distinct, so the exclusion silently fails to match. A file the maintainer intended to exclude is then packed into the `.tar.gz` and, if published, uploaded to the public, immutable PyPI index.  ## Details  File names in `FileList.files` come from `os.walk` (`setuptools/_distutils/filelist.py`, `_find_all_simple`), so on APFS a file written NFD is offered to the matcher in NFD, while the `MANIFEST.in` pattern carries the author's editor form (typically NFC). The matching path performs no canonicalization:  ```python # setuptools/command/egg_info.py  (FileList.global_exclude) def global_exclude(self, pattern):     match = translate_pattern(os.path.join('**', pattern))   # fnmatch.translate -> regex, no NFC/NFD     return self._remove_files(match.match)                   # byte-level regex over raw os.walk names ```  A rule written NFC (`café` = `63 61 66 c3 a9`) does not match an on-disk name written NFD (`café` = `63 61 66 65 cc 81`), even though the filesystem treats the two as one file.  A `unicodedata.normalize('NFD', ...)` helper exists in `setuptools/unicode_utils.py` (`decompose()`), but it is **never called in the manifest matching path**, so neither the pattern nor the walked path is normalized before matching. The only normalization in this area, `EggInfoCommand._manifest_normalize`, uses `filesys_decode` (bytes→str decode only, no NFC/NFD) and runs when writing `SOURCES.txt`, after matching has already occurred.  ## Impact  `MANIFEST.in` exclusions are the documented mechanism maintainers use to keep secrets, local configs, and private fixtures out of the published sdist. A non-ASCII excluded file may be published to the public, immutable PyPI index despite the rule — an irreversible disclosure with no visual cue (NFC and NFD forms render identically). Exposure is filesystem-dependent and most relevant on macOS APFS/HFS+, where many maintainers build and publish. Pure-ASCII rules are unaffected.  ## Proof of concept  With a project containing `MANIFEST.in`:  ``` global-include *.txt *.json global-exclude secret_café.txt    # rule saved NFC ```  and an on-disk file `secret_café.txt` written in NFD, `python -m build --sdist` packs the secret file into the resulting `.tar.gz`, while an ASCII control file excluded by the same directive is correctly dropped — isolating the bypass to the NFC-pattern vs. NFD-name mismatch. Reproduced on macOS APFS with setuptools 82.0.1.  ## Remediation  Normalize both the walked path and each `MANIFEST.in` pattern to a single canonical form before matching, in both `setuptools/command/egg_info.py` (`FileList`) and the vendored `setuptools/_distutils/filelist.py`. For an exclusion list, err toward excluding more, and document that `MANIFEST.in` matching is normalization-insensitive on macOS.  ## Credit  Reported by Tomas Illuminati. Coordinated via CERT/CC VINCE VU#604762.

### Summary  On Windows, attacker-controlled content in a wheel's `.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt` can cause setuptools' legacy wheel installation path to create an `__init__.py` outside the requested `destination_eggdir`.  The attacker can influence the destination path, but not the contents of the created file.  ### Details  Tested setuptools commit:  `6ead555c5fb29bc57fe6105b1bffc163f56fd558`  Relevant source:  `setuptools/wheel.py`  SHA-256:  `359b7e0d5dd8c3135653abe08a8ed5dc0352eadfd7df22cb5e2b5303b7c3cafd`  The relevant call path is:  `Wheel(wheel_path).install_as_egg(destination)` → `_install_as_egg` → `_convert_metadata` → `_fix_namespace_packages`  A wheel can provide attacker-controlled content in:  `<distribution>.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt`  The namespace value is eventually used approximately as:  ```python mod_dir = os.path.join(destination_eggdir, *mod.split('.')) mod_init = os.path.join(mod_dir, '__init__.py')  If mod is a Windows drive-qualified absolute path containing no dots, mod.split('.') preserves it as a single component. On Windows, os.path.join(destination_eggdir, absolute_component) discards the original base directory and resolves to the attacker-supplied absolute path. The existing wheel filename and ZIP traversal checks do not validate this metadata value before it is subsequently interpreted as a filesystem path.  ```markdown ### PoC  The reproduction was performed entirely inside a disposable temporary directory.  Layout:  ```text sandbox/     destination/     outside/     input/     canary.txt ```  A synthetic wheel was created containing:  `demo_pkg-1.0.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt`  whose content was the absolute path of:  `sandbox\outside`  The real acquired setuptools implementation was then invoked:  ```python setuptools.wheel.Wheel(synthetic_wheel).install_as_egg(     sandbox_destination ) ```  The operation completed without exception.  Expected metadata was created under:  `sandbox\destination\EGG-INFO`  but setuptools also created:  `sandbox\outside\__init__.py`  The file did not exist before execution.  Its contents were:  ```python __import__('pkg_resources').declare_namespace(__name__) ```  The unrelated canary remained byte-identical.  The sandbox was deleted after recording the evidence. ```   ### Impact  A crafted wheel can cause setuptools to create a fixed-content `__init__.py` outside the intended installation directory at a filesystem path influenced by the wheel, with the permissions of the process performing the installation.  The demonstrated reproduction required the target parent directory to already exist.

## Impact  urllib3's [streaming API](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/2.7.0/advanced-usage.html#streaming-and-i-o) is designed for efficiently handling large HTTP responses by reading the content in chunks, rather than loading the entire response body into memory at once. When decoding a [chunked-transfer-encoded response](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9112.html#chunked.encoding), this API reads each chunk's size field by buffering until it sees `\n` or EOF.  A malicious HTTP server can return `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and then send a very long run of bytes without any newline, causing the streaming client to buffer that entire run before urllib3 can reject the chunk size as invalid and allocate more memory than intended.  To fix the issue, we'll reject chunk-size fields larger than 65536 bytes, as already done in the non-streaming case, which is currently handled by the Python standard library. Note that this only applies to reading the chunk-size field, not the chunk data, which is already handled correctly. Thus, there shouldn't be any impact for non-malicious servers.  ## Affected usages  Applications and libraries using urllib3 versions earlier than 2.8.0 may be affected when streaming a chunked response from untrusted sources. Specifically, this affects the [read_chunked()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.read_chunked) and [stream()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.stream) methods of the HTTPResponse object.  This also affects requests streaming API, which uses urllib3 under the hood.  ## Remediation  Upgrade to urllib3 version 2.8.0 or later, where chunk-size fields larger than 65536 will be rejected. If upgrading is not immediately possible, consider reading the response at once using the [read()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.read) method.

### Impact  urllib3's streaming API is designed for the efficient handling of large HTTP responses by reading content in chunks instead of loading the entire response body into memory at once.  urllib3 can decompress response bodies according to the HTTP `Content-Encoding` header. When streaming a compressed, chunked response, urllib3 first consumes data already buffered by the decoder before reading the next HTTP chunk.  However, urllib3 versions from 2.6.2 through 2.7.0 could enter an infinite loop when a chunked response contained bytes after the end of the Deflate stream. If the decompressed body exceeded the requested streaming chunk size, Python's zlib implementation could retain the trailing bytes as unconsumed input after reaching the end of the compressed stream. urllib3 would repeatedly attempt to decode those same bytes without making progress or reading more data from the network.  A malicious server could exploit this behavior to cause excessive CPU usage and prevent the affected request from completing on the client. Network read timeouts would not interrupt the loop because no further socket operation was required.  ### Affected usages  Applications and libraries using urllib3 versions 2.6.2 through 2.7.0 may be affected when all of the following conditions are met:  1. Compressed responses from an untrusted source are streamed using `HTTPResponse.stream(amt=N)` or `HTTPResponse.read_chunked(amt=N)` with a positive, finite chunk size. 2. Content decoding is enabled. 3. The response uses both `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and `Content-Encoding: deflate`. 4. The decoded body exceeds the requested chunk size and the encoded body contains bytes after the end of the Deflate stream.  `HTTPResponse.stream()` uses a finite chunk size by default and is therefore affected when the other conditions are met.  ### Remediation  Upgrade to urllib3 2.8.0, in which the Deflate decoder stops accepting input after reaching the end of the compressed stream and no longer reports trailing bytes as data that can produce more decoded output.  If upgrading is not immediately possible, disable automatic content decoding for responses from untrusted sources by setting `decode_content=False`, or reject streamed responses using the Deflate content encoding. Applications that disable automatic decoding must handle the compressed response safely at another layer.

## Impact  urllib3 supports configuring TLS independently for an HTTPS proxy and the target server.  `proxy_ssl_context`, `proxy_assert_hostname`, and `proxy_assert_fingerprint` configure the TLS connection to the proxy. `ssl_context` and the other target-specific TLS parameters configure the connection to the target server.  In urllib3 versions 1.26.0 through 2.7.0, these configurations were not consistently separated. Depending on the proxy mode, urllib3 could:  1. Ignore `proxy_ssl_context` and use the target server's SSL context for the TLS connection to an HTTPS forwarding proxy. 2. Override the HTTPS proxy's certificate-verification policy with the target server's certificate-verification policy. 3. Apply target-specific SNI, hostname assertions, certificate fingerprint assertions, or TLS client credentials to the TLS connection to an HTTPS forwarding proxy.  In particular, configuring `cert_reqs="CERT_NONE"` for a target server could overwrite the `verify_mode` of the SSL context configured for the HTTPS proxy. This modification occurred in place and persisted on the context object, potentially disabling proxy certificate verification for later connections that reused the same context.  An attacker able to intercept the connection to an HTTPS proxy may be able to impersonate the proxy when the effective proxy TLS configuration disables certificate verification or otherwise accepts the attacker's certificate. This may occur, for example, when the target server's trust or identity policy is incorrectly applied to the proxy connection.  When HTTPS forwarding is enabled, an impersonated proxy can observe or modify forwarded requests and responses, potentially exposing credentials, authentication tokens, request bodies, response data, and other sensitive information.  A TLS client certificate intended for the target server may also be presented to the proxy or to an attacker impersonating it. This can disclose the client's identity and provide proof of possession of the corresponding private key. The private key itself is not transmitted during the TLS handshake.  In CONNECT tunneling mode, impersonating the HTTPS proxy does not by itself defeat the separate end-to-end TLS connection between the client and the target server.  ## Affected Usages  Code using urllib3 versions 1.26.0 through 2.7.0 may be affected in any of the following cases.  ### 1. The target SSL context is used for an HTTPS forwarding proxy  HTTPS requests are forwarded through an HTTPS proxy with `use_forwarding_for_https=True`, and `proxy_ssl_context` is configured for the proxy.  urllib3 may ignore `proxy_ssl_context` and use the target server's `ssl_context` for the proxy TLS handshake. The proxy may therefore be verified using the target server's trust and certificate policy instead of the policy explicitly configured for the proxy.  ### 2. The target verification policy overrides the proxy policy  An HTTPS proxy is configured with `proxy_ssl_context`, while the target server uses a different certificate-verification policy.  urllib3 may apply the target server's `cert_reqs` value to the proxy SSL context. For example, setting `cert_reqs="CERT_NONE"` for the target server may also disable certificate verification for the HTTPS proxy, even when `proxy_ssl_context` was configured to require verification.  This issue can affect the TLS connection to an HTTPS proxy in both forwarding and CONNECT tunneling configurations.  ### 3. A mutated proxy SSL context is reused  The same SSL context is reused as `proxy_ssl_context` across multiple connections, and certificate verification is disabled for one target server.  urllib3 may modify the proxy SSL context's `verify_mode` in place. Later connections that reuse the same context may therefore connect to the HTTPS proxy without certificate verification.  ### 4. Target-specific TLS identity or credentials are applied to the proxy  HTTPS requests are forwarded through an HTTPS proxy with `use_forwarding_for_https=True`, and target-specific SNI, hostname assertions, certificate fingerprint assertions, or TLS client credentials are configured.  urllib3 may apply these target-specific settings to the proxy TLS handshake. This may cause urllib3 to:  - send SNI intended for the target server to the proxy; - verify the proxy using a hostname or certificate fingerprint intended for the target server; or - present a TLS client certificate intended for the target server to the proxy.  Code connecting through a plain HTTP proxy does not establish a TLS connection to the proxy and is not affected by this issue.  ## Remediation  Upgrade to urllib3 2.8.0 or later.  urllib3 2.8.0 independently applies the explicitly configured `proxy_ssl_context` and proxy-specific certificate assertions to the HTTPS proxy connection. Target-specific SNI, certificate assertions, and TLS client certificate parameters are no longer applied to the HTTPS proxy handshake.  For backward compatibility, when an HTTPS proxy is used with `use_forwarding_for_https=True` and `proxy_ssl_context` is not provided, urllib3 2.8.0 continues to use `ssl_context` for the TLS connection to the proxy. This configuration emits a `FutureWarning`. In urllib3 3.0, passing `ssl_context` with `use_forwarding_for_https=True` for an HTTPS proxy will raise an error. Applications should use `proxy_ssl_context` to configure TLS for an HTTPS forwarding proxy.  The fixes were implemented in commits b6447295fff7b38fdffc67e0df9712d60cef3cc3 and 07408cec79d1856d81bb42c74a904a24fdb9e465.
